threads_text: Big US banks are catching AI agents logging into customer accounts with the customers' own passwords. The White House AI czar says that may break bank terms but is not a cyberattack, and floats read-only access as a middle ground. Would you give an AI agent your bank login?
caption:
Big US banks are catching third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, often logged in with the customer's own password.
White House AI czar David Sacks says it may break bank terms but is not a cyberattack.
Schwab and JPMorgan are blocking outside agents from moving money.

Would you give an AI agent your bank login?

site_article.headline: US banks find unauthorized AI agents in customer accounts as White House urges read-only access
site_article.dek: Customers are handing their logins to third-party AI agents, and banks including JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab are blocking those agents from moving money.
site_article.summary: Major US banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating in customers' online accounts, according to an Axios report described by CBS News on October 23, 2026. White House AI czar David Sacks said the activity may violate bank terms but is not a cyberattack, and suggested read-only access as a middle ground.
site_article.seo_title: Banks find unauthorized AI agents in customer accounts
site_article.seo_description: Major US banks are detecting third-party AI agents in customer accounts. David Sacks says it is not a cyberattack; banks block agents from moving money.
site_article.answer_summary: Customers are giving their bank usernames and passwords to AI agents the banks have not vetted. Banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab let some outside tools read account data but block them from moving money.
site_article.hero_alt: Photo of JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon.

paragraphs.text: Major banks in the United States are detecting unauthorized activity from third-party AI agents operating inside customers' online accounts, according to an Axios report described by CBS News on October 23, 2026. Axios senior AI reporter Madison Mills told CBS News the problem is industrywide and affects dozens of financial institutions.

According to Mills, the activity usually starts with the customers themselves. People hand their usernames and passwords to AI agents that their bank has not vetted, which breaks the terms of service that banks set for online accounts. In some cases, the agents then took steps the account holder had not approved, such as calling a bank to file a complaint.
Mills said the agents were not hacking into accounts or draining funds. In her description, they were largely doing what their users had asked them to do, only without the permission of the bank.

David Sacks, the White House AI czar, responded on X. He drew a line between agents that users authorize and rogue agents that could be used in cyberattacks, writing that the activity described may violate bank terms but is not a cyberattack. Sacks suggested banks could give agents read-only access as a middle ground, and described full write access, which lets an agent act on an account, as a riskier category.

JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon addressed outside agents on the bank's third quarter earnings call on October 13. He said the bank would not let just any outside agent inside the company and warned about rogue agents, which he said could number in the thousands. A bank spokeswoman told Cybernews that JPMorgan does not allow third parties to log in with customers' banking credentials. Outside tools can view some account data in read-only form but cannot move money or pay bills.

Charles Schwab chief executive Rick Wurster told Bloomberg Television on October 16 that the firm blocks unauthorized AI agents that try to move client money, including Meta's Muse personal agent, according to The Next Web. Schwab receives a weekly report on these blocks. Wurster said the core worry is clients giving their passwords to an agent that then acts for them, which leaves open the question of who is liable if something goes wrong.

Schwab plans to give outside AI tools read-only access through model context protocol servers, so they can check balances and run research without moving money. The firm also wants clients to use its own assistant, Charley, which it announced on September 30.

PYMNTS reported that Citigroup does not let third-party agents log in to accounts or make transactions, while some authorized open banking providers can retrieve account information in read-only form. Bank of America chief executive Brian Moynihan said on October 14 that a human should approve money leaving an account. Morgan Stanley told CBS News it has not seen unauthorized AI agent activity on its platforms, and a Chase spokesperson advised customers not to share their login credentials with anyone.

The pattern across these responses is a split between reading and acting. Banks appear willing to let AI tools see account data through approved channels, but none of the large banks named in these reports allows an outside agent to move money on a customer's behalf. The Sacks proposal sits close to where those banks already are, which suggests read-only access could become the default arrangement while the question of liability stays unsettled.

The next signal to watch is whether a major bank publishes a formal way for customers to connect an AI agent with limited permissions, or whether regulators set rules on who pays when an authorized agent makes a costly mistake.
